items.title: Ricard Alexis Interview, 1959-01-16
items.q: Louis Armstrong was a very poor reader. Very poor. Couldn't even sign his name. When I was getting the letter from Louis Armstrong and saw the nights he stretched his name down like that. I was surprised.

ctx.x: How did he play before he went to Chicago? Was he pretty good or rough or good tone? No, he was clean.

He was good tone. Good tone. Wonderful tone. Variation, beautiful variation and things like that. But I never told him about reading. Well, just like Rene, like I told you, P. Rowe was starting that job on the Rube garden and he had Rene and I to show up to see which one he wanted. He tried both of us on the rehearsal. He wronged and took me. Rene and I showed him and he went on to find his business with his home. He couldn't read fast enough. Louis Armstrong was a very poor reader. Very poor. Couldn't even sign…

items.title: Ricard Alexis Interview, 1959-01-16
items.q: Red bean and rice in the yours, Nurse Armstrong.

ctx.x: I'm going to show you how he edited his letters. We used to get kicks out of it.

Red bean and rice in the yours, Nurse Armstrong. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth. And now that I wrote a letter from him, I see how he scratched his name down there. Like a business man. I said, wow, he went to win at school. He writes nice. I've seen him write. I don't know. I'd like to ask Lawrence Morrero. He knows. Don't forget to get these. I think they're in that between his friends, Johnson and Galbraith. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth. I'm going to show you how to tell the truth.…
And now that I'm going to put a letter from him and I see how he scratched his name down there. I'm like a business man. I said, wow, he went to win at school. He writes nice. I've seen him write.
